speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity of reporting on the progress of grain deliveries in the prairie provinces and advising the house of certain quota changes which will become effective at an early date. I am glad to report that up until the close of business on December 1, producers' deliveries of all grains in the west amounted to about 259 million bushels. With some space now available in country elevators in all three provinces and with car loadings running at a high level, I am confident that the objective of grain deliveries for the August-December period will be realized. With actual deliveries of about 260 million bushels up to Deceember 2, I am confident that producers will have the opportunity of marketing well over 300 million bushels by the close of the present calendar year.
I would now like to advise the house that the Canadian wheat board is today announcing an increase in delivery quotas to take effect on December 14. I might add that this fall and especially during the past few weeks the railway companies, in co-operation with the transport controller and the Canadian wheat board, have been endeavouring to provide sufficient space at all delivery points to enable producers to complete delivery of their initial quota and the supplementary quota for oats, along with deliveries for which special permits have been issued by the board.
Although this objective is not entirely reached yet, considerable progress has been made and at many points the required space has been provided along with some excess space. The railway companies have been requested to continue preferential car supply at delivery points where space is still required

Inquiries of the Ministry for delivery quotas presently in effect and it is anticipated that these remaining points will be taken care of before the end of the present month. Having this fact in mind and the possibility of a change in weather and road conditions, the wheat board considers it desirable that an increase in delivery quotas should take place at the earliest possible date.
The increase in delivery quotas which is being announced by the board today provides for a second quota of two bushels per specified acre at all delivery points effective on December 14. The second delivery quota is subject to a minimum delivery of 300 bushels; that is, under the second quota producers may deliver two bushels per specified acre or 300 bushels, whichever is the higher.
I think the provision of minimum deliveries under quotas this year is very important. Members will recall that under the initial quota the minimum delivery of 500 bushels was provided for and this was later increased to 700 bushels. With the provision of a minimum delivery of 700 bushels against the initial quota and the minimum delivery of 300 bushels against the second quota, all producers have now been authorized to deliver a minimum of 1,000 bushels of grain under the combined initial and second quotas.
While the new delivery quota will not become effective until December 14, the board has made provision whereby elevator agents at delivery points which now have adequate space may apply to the board for earlier permission to accept deliveries from local producers up to two bushels per specified acre, these deliveries applying against the second quota which will become effective on December 14.
I might also add that the transport controller has announced the lifting of the suspension of the operation of car order books effective from December 14, 1953. The house will recall that the car order book was suspended on October 19, 1953, as a measure to facilitate the shipment of grain and grades of grain required to meet market requirements. As from December 14 the operation of car order books will again be restored.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last few days there have been a number of exchanges between the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) and myself with respect to a recent

The Address-Mr. Knowles ruling of the tariff board concerning the 10 per cent sales tax as applied to apparatus used for the production of electricity. I do not intend to spend very long on this question, but there is underlying it an issue which I feel to be of great importance, and I think it should be brought before the house with the least possible delay.
The immediate and most obvious issue, Mr. Speaker, is of course the question as to whether this particular type of machinery is to be exempt from the 10 per cent sales tax. That immediate issue is of concern not only to the particular company which was the appellant before the tariff board, but it is of interest to farmers and others who are purchasers of this kind of machinery. But there is more involved in this issue than just the question of whether or not this particular type of machinery is to be subject to the sales tax. The deeper and more fundamental issue is this. Is the law of this country to be defined and set out clearly so the citizens of Canada will know what it is; or is it to be made by ad hoc decisions by a minister of the cabinet or by some deputy or civil servant to whom that minister delegates his authority?
For the suggestion I have already made to the effect that this matter is being dealt with in the wrong way I rely on a ruling made by the tariff board under date of November 24, 1953, and also on certain extremely interesting sections of the proceedings of the tariff board. The proceedings I have in my hand are those of October 28, 1953.
The particulars of the case briefly are these. A certain company in Canada which makes power plants for the production of electricity and makes these power plants available for use on farms as well as in other places, applied to the Department of National Revenue for those power plants to be exempt from the sales tax under the provisions of schedule III of the Excise Tax Act. The Department of National Revenue denied that request. Thereupon the company appealed that decision to the tariff board.
A good deal of the discussion of this case before the tariff board turned on the question of whether or not the minister had carried out the provisions of the Excise Tax Act. As a matter of fact the judgment of the tariff board on that point can be found in these words from the decision or declaration of the board:
As regards the minister's obligation to define "machinery and apparatus'', there is no evidence in the record that it has ever been defined.
When this question was before the tariff board there appeared on behalf of the government, or on behalf of the Department of


National Revenue, counsel from the Department of Justice. The name of the lawyer in question was Mr. D. H. W. Henry and his submission, of course, was that the decision of the Department of National Revenue should be upheld. But during the discussion questions were asked him about the meaning of the pertinent part of schedule III of the Excise Tax Act; and Mr. Henry said to the tariff board, on the date I have already indicated, that the wording of the section, after he had quoted it-
-indicates that it was the intention of parliament that the minister should in the first place make regulation-in other words that he would exercise a legislative function in defining what the expression "machinery and apparatus" means.
Mr. Buchanan, a member of the board, interrupted at that point and said:
I am wondering if that definition of "machinery and apparatus" is available.
The chairman said:
Or put it another way. Did he ever define, and if so, at large or in a specific instance?
Then Mr. Henry, counsel from the Department of Justice, representing the Department of National Revenue before the tariff board, said:
My instructions are that there is no general definition that has been made by the minister of the first branch of this provision-namely: what is "machinery and apparatus"?
Then after the matter was discussed a little further Mr. Henry, counsel for the defendant, if you please, said this:
Again, if X may continue with the answer to Mr. Buchanan's question, the opinion may be formed in particular cases but in my submission it was primarily intended by parliament to form part of the general rules laid down by the minister.
In other words Mr. Henry, who was representing the government, admitted that it was clearly the intention of parliament as it was put in the act that the minister should first of all define this class of "machinery and apparatus" so that citizens applying for exemption from sales tax would know what definition their particular articles had to meet. At that point Mr. Buchanan again entered the discussion and said:
That would at least put them in a position to understand where they are in these matters. That is exactly mv question. If these things are to be done on an ad hoc basis every time anybody makes an importation of "machinery and apparatus" he is going to do it in ignorance of the state of the law.
Right there, Mr. Speaker, is the nub of the real issue in this case. In this country we believe in the rule of law. We believe in laws being spelled out so that all may know what they provide. In particular in this type of law, the general practice is that the

average citizen will know what the law is and what the definition is that his particular article may have to meet. In this instance we find there has not even yet been any general definition of "machinery and apparatus" as is required by the Excise Tax Act. The situation is rather that the Minister of National Revenue, either on his own or on the recommendation of the people in his department, is making a decision on an ad hoc basis with respect to each application that comes along. Later in this same discussion before the tariff board the chairman said this:
If it has not been made public-
That is the list of ad hoc decisions.
-it simply amounts to the fact that there are in the files of the department a number of decisions.

Again Mr. Henry, counsel from the Department of Justice.
-It may be that you will come to the conclusion that in the absence of regulations of a general nature to which a taxpayer may refer, that the conditions required as a prerequisite under this section have not been fulfilled. That is a matter for the board to decide.
On that point, Mr. Speaker, in its declaration of November 24, 1953 the board expressed its opinion. Its opinion was that the minister had not carried out the requirement of the act to spell out this definition first so that all comers might know what was the definition, the test which their articles would have to meet.
In the questions and answers that we have had across the floor of the house since last Friday the minister has said that it is difficult to meet the requirement of the act. In fact he went further and said that it is impossible to spell out such a definition in advance. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is no more an answer to the requirement of an act of parliament than was the answer which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) made when we criticized him for disobeying a requirement of the Combines Investigation Act a few years ago. Surely laws passed by parliament are laws and their requirements are to be met not only by the humblest citizens of the land but by the Minister of Justice and by the Minister of National Revenue.
It may be that the Minister of National Revenue can demonstrate to parliament that the wording of that act in its present form presents a difficulty or even an insurmountable barrier. If so, I submit that his course is to come back to parliament and ask for a change in the wording of the act in order 83276-37
The Address-Mr. Knowles to put it on a workable basis. But my reading of the proceedings of the hearing before the tariff board, Mr. Speaker, and my reading of the declaration made by the board lead me to feel that these gentlemen were of the opinion that it was possible to have such a definition in advance, and that therefore the will of parliament in that regard should be adhered to by the minister. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I strongly urge that the government reconsider its position with respect to this matter.
I am concerned about the immediate issue as well. It seems to me that power plants for the production of electricity on farms should be exempt from the sales tax. Incidentally, yesterday when the Minister of National Revenue was replying to one of my questions on this matter, he referred to this apparatus as being used in connection with summer resorts and motels. I take it that it was only a slip in the rush of answering the question that led the minister to omit a reference to farms. I place emphasis upon that, and suggest that power plants for the production of electricity for use on farms should, as a matter of common sense and fairness and in the light of the terms of the act, be exempt from the sales tax.

speechtext:
But there is now some doubt, and I hope the whole question of the application of the sales tax to such articles will be reviewed. But as I have already indicated in what I have said thus far, to me an even more important issue is the question as to how ministers of the crown regard and treat acts of parliament. It is not good enough for them to say they are not going to carry out this section or that because it is impossible or because another minister advises them not to do so. The rule of law is too sacred and important to democracy for it to be put aside lightly in that way.
I had thought of leaving this matter until we got to the minister's estimates or to a discussion of the Excise Tax Act later in the session, but the more I thought it over the more it seemed to me there was an obligation that I must fulfil, namely that I should raise the matter now at least to this extent so it might be aired in this way, and so the minister might have time to think it over and make the necessary corrections. I do not ask him to rely on my statement of the case, although I think it is a fair one, but I do urge him to study very carefully the opinions expressed by the tariff board; and I think he should read again, as I have no doubt he has already done, the representations made by Mr. Henry on his behalf and

The Address-Mr. Knowles the views which Mr. Henry expressed as to what the Excise Tax Act requires. Let us remember all through the piece that the rule of law is very important to democracy.
There is another matter on which I wish to say a few words at this time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
I am very glad to do that, and I do so in relation to tbe minister's statement of yesterday when he said the tariff board upheld the decision of the department. I suppose it is the minister's desire now that I put on the record the part of the declaration that seems to bear out his contention of yesterday, but which I do not think is really telling the whole story. The last two paragraphs are the ones the minister wants me to put on the record, I believe, and I may say in advance that it will take some thinking on the part of hon. members to realize what they mean. They read as follows:
However, it seems clear that the minister never expressed an opinion relative to "machinery and apparatus to be used directly in the production of" electricity.
Remember, the board has already said he should have done so.
If, as counsel for the appellant argues, the minister cannot "look through" electricity to other goods, then all foregoing expressions of ministerial opinion are nullities.
Keep in mind that "all foregoing expressions of ministerial opinion are nullities". I go on:
The consequence of such a finding must be that the electric generating sets at issue, and, indeed, all other electric generating sets, are subject to tax. If, on the other hand, the minister can "look through" electricity to other "goods", his expression of opinion is clear and the electric generating sets at issue are not within the exemption.
Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed.
Hon. members can pore over that and figure out what it means. I have done so. I have pored over the whole declaration of the board, and the evidence and proceedings at the sitting of the board, and I think it is a fair summary to say that what the board did was not to uphold the decision of the minister that these goods were subject to tax but rather to dismiss the appeal of the company on the ground that there was nothing before it against which they could test the particular class of goods the company wanted to have exempted.

All the way through the piece they point out that there is no definition as required by the act and nothing against which to test these goods. Therefore the board had no option but to render a decision not upholding the decision of the minister to apply the tax but dismissing the appeal of the appellant because there was really nothing on which the appellant could base that appeal. Why is there nothing on which he can base an appeal? Because the minister has not spelled out the definition required by the act of parliament. In other words, as Mr. McKinnon, the chairman of the board, said during the course of the discussion, it is unsatisfactory for people not to know in advance what the law is.
I repeat my appeal to the minister and also to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson)- I am glad to note his interest in this legal question-to give further study to the matter in the light of something with which we all agree, namely that the rule of law should prevail.
As I said a moment ago, there is another matter on which I should like to say something at this time. It too arises out of exchanges across the floor of the house during questions on the orders of the day. Yesterday on the orders of the day I put a certain question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) arising out of the fact that the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada had presented its brief to the federal government at noon yesterday. I will not say anything more about the nature of the answer the Minister of National Health and Welfare gave me yesterday. My leader said he found it difficult to understand what the minister was saying, and I think many other people were in the same boat.
But I would call to the attention of the house that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) had something to say with respect to the same matter, namely the appeal of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada for health insurance. The Prime Minister met a delegation from that labour body yesterday. With respect to the question of health insurance itself the Prime Minister made the usual answer we get from Liberals so often, namely that one has to consider the position of the provinces, the cost of the proposition and so on. I have dealt with those phases of the matter a good many times before and probably will do so a good many times in the future, at any rate until we get legislation on this matter.
But the particular phase of the matter which the Prime Minister dealt with yesterday that really concerned me was this refusal

to agree even to the request of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada that a special parliamentary committee be set up at this session to go into the whole question of health insurance. The government knows, and hon. members know, that we are fully aware of what can on occasion be the result of sending a subject to a committee. At times it may simply mean that it is shelved, but there have been occasions when the house has done exceptionally good work through the medium of committees. Veterans affairs committees of bygone sessions are particularly outstanding examples of the work private members of parliament can do when they get together and are given a certain amount of latitude to go into a question and deal with it on its merits.
Another instance where a good job was done by private members was the committee on old age security in 1950. I mention it because I am told that the Prime Minister made reference to it yesterday when he was answering the representations of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. I was not present at that meeting, but I am informed that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) told the delegates that as a result of the deliberations of the committee on old age security in 1950, and as a result of the report and recommendations they made to the house, the government felt itself at that time to be at least under a moral obligation to carry out the recommendations of that committee. Apparently, because of that experience, the Prime Minister told the labour people yesterday that he was fearful-that is the word in quotation marks in the Canadian Press dispatch in the Gazette this morning-of sending the question of health insurance to a committee of this house.
I am not surprised at his being fearful, Mr. Speaker, but I am surprised at the Prime Minister admitting it, admitting that he is fearful of sending the question of health insurance to a committee. Why do I say I am not surprised that that is his feeling? I say that because of what happened in 1950. All of us who were here will recall that some of us were fighting hard, with a great deal of public support, to get rid of the means test from the old age pension. When the suggestion was made that a committee should be established many of us were afraid it was simply a means of shelving the issue. I recall those debates very well, and it was clear to me at the time that it was the government's thought the committee would simply find that it was too costly to remove the means test from old age pensions, and that it could not be done unless we inaugurated the insurance principle involving contributions by individuals into personal accounts.
The Address-Mr. Knowles
Though that was apparently what the government thought the committee on old age security would find, and that on the basis of that finding the issue would be shelved, the committee did not make that finding. The committee did a very good job, and I say that for the members of all parties on the committee. I would even say that for the representatives from the other place who were on the committee. In addition to the freedom we had as individual members, and in addition to the excellent study that was made of the question by hon. members, we had the best advice obtainable on this question from the deputy minister of welfare and the other officials from that department, particularly from the research division of that department. They were exceedingly able people; they had the material, and on the basis of their material we were able to make a thorough study of this question.
As a result of that thorough and useful study the idea of recommending the strict insurance principle was rejected. Instead, we recommended back to parliament that we have a system of universal old age pensions, and that the collection of the funds necessary for old age pensions be on a taxation basis. In other words we recommended pensions as of right, paid for according to ability to pay. As I say, the work of that committee is in a class with the work of the veterans affairs committee, in that it did an excellent job and brought back a very valuable report. The plain fact of the matter is that it was such a good report, and it had such wide popular support, the government found itself in the position of having to consider the recommendations of the committee. In due course those recommendations were implemented in their main outlines, and they are now on the statute books of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, may I as a newcomer to the House of Commons be permitted to add my voice to those who, in such glowing terms, paid tribute to those sterling qualities which so admirably fit you for the carrying out of your highly responsible duties as Speaker of this house. I am impressed by your wisdom and impartiality in your adjudication thus far. May I extend to you my sincere congratulations and wish you every success in your new duties.
May I take this opportunity also to compliment the hon. members for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) and Roberval (Mr. Ville-neuve), mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, upon making a very worth-while contribution. May I also congratulate the lady members upon their election to the House of Commons. I am sure they will have many gems of wisdom to pass on to this house during this session.
I deem it a very great honour to have been elected by the people of Jasper-Edson constituency to represent them in this twenty-second parliament of Canada. I am deeply conscious of the tremendous responsibilities that go hand in hand with this high honour. I feel most humble and grateful to the people of my constituency for their expression of confidence, and I shall do everything within my power to justify it.
The constituency of Jasper-Edson is one of the largest and perhaps the most diversified of constituencies, both from the viewpoint of industry and topography, changing as it does from the level and fertile farm areas in the east, gradually running into the foothills and finally reaching the rugged grandeur of the Rockies. Although agriculture is perhaps the greatest industry of all, embracing as it does grain farming, dairying and stock raising,


because of the tremendous development in oil and natural gas this whole area is becoming more and more pockmarked with oil and gas wells, which add materially to the economy of the area.
We have millions of feet of first-grade lumber being manufactured each year, and there are many thousands of acres of virgin timber yet to be cut. We have unlimited deposits of the finest steam coal to be found anywhere, and in Jasper national park we have one of the masterpieces of nature. There you find the grandeur of the snow-capped mountains, the breathtaking beauty of lakes and canyons, a profusion of beautiful wildflowers, an abundance of wildlife and rivers teeming with all types of game fish. All these beauties along with her gigantic icefields have made Jasper national park truly a paradise which annually attracts thousands of tourists from all parts of the world, thus making the tourist trade a very vital and important factor in our national economy.
I was keenly interested in the forecast of proposed government legislation which was outlined in the speech from the throne, the indication of the need of further assistance in the matter of housing and the intention of the government to give assistance to the physically handicapped. Both these matters are of great concern to the constituents of Jasper-Edson, as they are to the citizen of Canada as a whole.
I was greatly impressed with the many fine arguments presented on behalf of the physically handicapped, whether it be through old age, blindness, war disability or physical handicaps of some other nature, and the almost unanimous recognition on all sides of the house that something must be done about it. I concur wholeheartedly with them. It should be the main purpose of government to look after those members of our society who are unfortunate and handicapped, for it is my belief that the individual and his wellbeing represent the greatest asset of our country, and every citizen is entitled to protection against the hazards of life and old age. The lack of adequate assistance to these fine people is shocking and a disgrace. With our country literally bursting at the seams with the essentials of life, and billions of dollars being provided each year for armaments, comparatively little or nothing is being done for our aged and handicapped and underprivileged. It surely is a strange paradox.
I have listened with interest to the many eloquent appeals on behalf of the fishermen, the fruit growers, the coal miners, the textile workers, the lumbermen and the farmers and their storage problems. I recognize that

they have many grave problems. It is becoming more obvious to thinking people that we may expect this condition to continue until this government recognizes that the consumer must be given more purchasing power for local consumption, and until there is a willingness on the part of this government to trade on a basis of mutual advantage and to accept sterling from other trading nations.
These things have been discussed at some length, so I do not at this point propose to take up time in discussing them further. But there are one or two things I should like to discuss briefly that play a very important part in the economy of the farmer and the consuming public as well. I bring to this house 42 years of experience in the retail meat trade, and feel that what I have to say in this regard comes from the school of experience rather than from just trying to be critical. I refer of course to the unfair practices of the meat packing industry.
There was a time in the packing industry when there was some semblance of compatibility between the livestock prices and the wholesale prices of the finished product, but not any more. During the last war we had price controls which helped, but now they have thrown discretion to the winds and are out to take the public for all the traffic will bear. The quality of their products in many cases has deteriorated, and the wholesale prices do not reflect any relationship between rail grade price and the wholesale price.
For example, let me go back to last Easter. Most of you know there is an extra demand for smoked ham at this season of the year. Let us see what happened. About the time the butchers were thinking of ordering their Easter hams, bingo; up went the price of smoked hams 8 cents a pound overnight. But on checking the rail grade price we found that that same day the rail grade price had dropped 65 cents a hundred.
I have seen the prices of cooked ham and bacon go up as much as 10 cents a pound overnight, in one instance at least, with little or no justification for it. Can the minister or anyone else tell me why this should be? Can he tell me why, with top rail grade prices ranging from 284 cents to around 34 cents, cooked hams should sell for $1.02 or $1.04 or $1.06 a pound wholesale, depending on how much they thought the trade would pay, or why sliced back bacon should be sold at 95 cents a pound wholesale under similar rail grade prices?
You will have quite a job to sell me the idea that these wholesale prices were necessary to make a good margin of profit when the rail grade prices were at the level I quoted. The same thing happens with beef.
The Address-Mr. Yuill The farmer is again at the mercy of the packers and has to take almost anything they want to offer, particularly if he has an off-grade type animal; but in spite of this it invariably finds its way well up the grade when offered for sale at wholesale.
There is also an inevitable law that when there is a decline in hog prices and public sentiment demands a reduction of say 2 cents a pound, it is a safe bet that the price of beef automatically goes up 2 cents without fail. I suppose it is their usual good reasoning, that what we lose on the peanuts we make on the bananas.
These things are happening and I do not have to go outside my own shop to prove it. They try to justify their action by the old story of supply and demand. Assuming that they are right, do you not think the farmer should be allowed to enjoy some of the fruits of his labour and share in this increase?
There is another thing that causes some concern to the farmers in my constituency.
It is the attitude shown by this government during the period of the foot-and-mouth disease. This epidemic was perhaps no fault of the government, nor do I quarrel with the way they controlled and finally stamped it out, but what puzzles the farmer is why he was not considered when it came to this question of price support.
The farmers were told, by inference at any rate, that there was nothing to worry about, that they would still receive the basic floor price of around 23 cents and that then all would be well. But imagine their surprise and disappointment when they sold their heavy hogs, into the raising of which they had put all their extra grain and a great deal of labour, for as low as 114 cents a pound, or only 50 per cent of the price they expected. The government then turned around and paid the packers 60 cents a pound to process hogs for which in some cases they had paid only 114 cents. Surely the farmers should have received the subsidy. I suggest that the government take immediate steps to check and put a stop to these unfair practices, for one can readily see how such practices affect the purchasing power of the consuming public.
One other thing I feel should be stressed is the importance of our tourist trade. Tourists in ever-increasing numbers have been visiting Jasper national park from all parts of the world. They spend large sums of money in this country. It is not all spent in our national parks, but it is spread all across the country and sooner or later finds its way into our national economy. Many of these tourists comment on the lack of trans-Canada highways; they are amazed that a country the size of Canada has no trans-Canada highways.

The Address-Mr. Yuill These tourists think perhaps only in terms of their own convenience, but the need is very obvious. Every day we hear about the urgency and the necessity of civil defence. Millions of dollars are being spent every year in this way; yet if we were attacked from the west coast we have scarcely a highway on which to transport men and munitions.
Through my constituency runs the proposed Yellowhead route which, if built, I am sure will be one of the most serviceable and economical routes in western Canada. Apart from its strategic importance in the event of war, it would prove a boon to the tourist trade and of great advantage to the residents along that route. It is important that this highway be built as soon as possible.
In the town of Jasper we have a problem that is perhaps common to all towns within the national park; that is the problem of providing hospital and nursing services for the tourists and residents of the town and the surrounding area. Like many other places the demand in Jasper for these services grew to a point where the present unit proved inadequate and a new wing had to be built at a cost of some $70,000. This hospital, known as the Seton hospital, is privately administered by the Sisters of Seton of Halifax.
In view of the fact that Jasper is a ward of the federal parks administration and therefore not recognized as a municipality by the provincial government, it must forgo any municipal hospital building grants, and for some reason it has not received any building grant from the federal authorities in the same way that hospitals do elsewhere. This makes their financial position very precarious indeed, and it would seem only fair that they should receive favourable consideration, especially in the light of the fact that a large sum of money was spent in the building of a swimming pool in Jasper a short time ago. Surely this hospital and nursing service should receive a grant sufficient to make it the boon to humanity it was designed to be.
In general, the federal authorities should give greater attention and more assistance to this great resort centre. The development of the tourist trade is the best way to promote good will, and it is one of our greatest sources of revenue. This is borne out by the fact that 26,276,834 tourists visited Canada in 1952 and spent $275 million. I believe this revenue would be greatly increased, certainly in Jasper national park, if we had a Yellow-head trans-Canada highway to serve the people of western Canada from coast to coast, less regimentation of the businessmen catering to the needs of these people, and more assistance in providing hospital and nursing services for all.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to indicate certain views in regard to the amendment to the amendment which is now before the house. During the course of discussions that have taken place several ministers have availed themselves of the opportunity to place before the house explanations in regard to the activities of their own departments. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) on more than one occasion has explained to us various aspects of the problems with which he is directly connected. I wish only to refer to one remark he made earlier this week, which I would not wish to let pass without comment if only because there sometimes is a tendency to accept a statement which has not been answered as though the statement itself were not challenged.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke about his confidence as compared with the pessimists. I must admit without hesitation that he did not define the pessimists. However, by inference, he left a very clear suggestion as to who the pessimists were when he said the opposition had something in the nature of a vested interest in depression.
May I point out that confidence in Canada, confidence in the future and in our immense opportunities, is not the exclusive privilege of the Liberal party, nor has there been any suggestion in any of the speeches that have been made by members of the Conservative party that we have not at least as great confidence and, in some respects, I believe a great deal more in the possibility of the expansion of this extremely fortunate land of ours. It is no evidence of fear about the future to deal with weak spots in our economy and suggest that it is the responsibility of government to recognize these situations and deal with them in every way within the power of the government.
We have pointed out certain problems which the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself readily admits do exist. I grant that they are not interpreted as being unduly serious in the remarks of the minister. He passes rather lightly over the problem of the accumulation of wheat. He passes very lightly over the situation in the textile industry. He deals in very casual terms with the problems confronting our cheese

producers and our other agricultural producers who have been so seriously affected by the curtailment of sales. That procedure, I concede, is perfectly natural.
One might not expect him to go too far in admitting that the warnings which have been uttered for some time in this house have now been more than justified by events. But let me say most emphatically that the Conservative party believes in the future of Canada. We believe that the way to avoid difficulties is to expand the resources of our country and give employment to Canadians by the use of our own resources in every way that is humanly possible. Wherever we have pointed to difficulties or to situations that should be faced, it has been only with the thought that we do not want to see the forward march of this great country of ours interrupted unnecessarily at any time by avoidable difficulties which now present themselves in different forms.
I am not going to enlarge upon these remarks except to say once again that most certainly an examination of the record this session and during preceding sessions will not justify any suggestion that we lack faith in the future of this great nation or in the immense opportunities that are open to the people of this country if under a free enterprise system the energy, the initiative and the skill of hard-working men and women are rewarded in the way they can be rewarded under a system of free enterprise, or free competition, call it what you will.
I wish now to deal as briefly as I can with a subject I mentioned in my opening speech in this debate. The national film board is an essential part of the cultural and educational life of Canada. It performs extremely useful services, and it supplies excellent films to the thousands of outlets where these films can be shown. Many of the films produced by the film board are used for educational purposes in every province of Canada. To that extent at least it can be said there has been a decision by parliament. However, there is no opportunity for orderly debate, for examination of any records or for an understanding of what the policy of the government really is. The government waits in pained impatience for the opposition to exhaust itself. Then in due course that exhaustion becomes a reality. The work of the board in Ottawa should be centralized and suitable accommodation provided.
There was no suggestion that it would be advisable to move the board to some other place. May I repeat:
The work of the board in Ottawa should be centralized and suitable accommodation provided.
This subject had been discussed at a meeting of the national film board committee on June 3 of last year. At that time the chairman of the national film board gave his evidence to the committee. He was asked the following question by Mr. Browne, the former member for St. John's West, as appears at page 88 of the proceedings of the committee: "Are the plans made?" To this the chairman of the board answered, "No, the plans are not finished." A further question was asked:
They are going to Montreal instead of remaining in Ontario?
The chairman answered, "That is the policy." Then the question was asked:
What is the reason for locating in Montreal?
To this the chairman replied:
That is a matter of policy, sir, and I do not know whether or not I should review it.
I am referring to this matter again today, Mr. Speaker, not alone to emphasize the justification for my repeated request that this matter be referred back to the house or a committee thereof, but also to give vivid evidence of the kind of information we get about these sacred cows once they have been created. No one is raising any question about the desirability of setting up an

organization of this kind, but we do object to the suggestion of sanctity which immediately surrounds these publicly-owned bodies and makes it an almost indescribable offence to raise any question at all as to how their business is carried on.
Just think of it. Just last year it was asked: "Are the plans made?" "No, they are not finished." Yet this is a matter the house is supposed to have decided. The chairman was asked if they were going to Montreal, and he said that was the policy. He was asked why, and he said it was a matter of policy and he did not know whether he should review it. There the matter rested, and that was all the information that was really available.
Now we come to the present year. On February 13 of this year it was definitely stated for the first time that it had been decided to move the operating sections of the national film board to the Montreal area, and that a site was in process of acquisition by the Department of Public Works in Ville St. Laurent. These were the words of the minister on February 13, as recorded at page 1906 of Hansard:
. . . it has been decided to move the operating sections of the national film board to the Montreal area, and a site has been acquired by the Department of Public Works in Ville St. Laurent. Plans are presently being completed and it is proposed that construction of the building will start later this year.
At least it was indicated then that the decision had been made. On February 26 the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) was pointing out the various items about which we should have known a great deal more than we did at that time, and in regard to which there was every possibility that economies could have been effected without in any way impairing the efficiency of the operation. In an excellent speech he dealt with a number of items reviewing the broad field of government expenditure. At that time the hon. member asked a question which was designed to find out what had happened. The answer was given at page 2415 of Hansard for February 26, 1953, in these words:
No price has yet been offered.
In other words the acquisition had not then reached the point where any price had been offered; that was on February 26 of this year. The subject came up for discussion briefly on March 12, 1953, when the hon. member for Kamloops indicated the need for further information. He made this statement appearing at page 2869 of Hansard for March 12, 1953:
Eut I question very much whether the people of this country would be prepared to consent to the spending of $5,225,000 to build a central office for the film board in Montreal. I wonder if it would 83276-381
The Address-Mr. Drew
not be possible to establish an adequate central office without spending nearly five and a quarter million dollars?
That seemed like a reasonable question to direct to the government and to the house. The very form in which the question of the hon. member for Kamloops was framed indicates how little information was available to the members of this house last spring when the very limited discussion took place which is to be found in the records.
The most revealing questions and answers are found in Hansard for April 9, 1953. I refer to them particularly because it was to the comments on April 9 that the Prime Minister referred as "discussion" on this subject. May I indicate just how much real discussion there was. In fact, it sounds a little like Alice in Wonderland. When the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser), who has been one of the most ardent supporters of the film board on either side of the house, was trying to get certain information about what was taking place, he asked the Minister of Public Works the following questions. These questions and answers are recorded at page 3645 of Hansard for April 9, 1953:
Is it the intention of the government to proceed with that building this year?
Now, having regard to the statements made outside the house that this matter has been decided by parliament, may I ask the members to really think of the amount of information contained in the reply of the Minister of Public Works. These are his words as recorded on the same page of Hansard:
I am not too sure that we have completed purchase of the site. I think somebody raised that question earlier in the session and I answered that we were negotiating with two or three parties who are the owners of the site.
The hon. member for Peterborough proceeded to question the minister with the tenacity he exhibits in regard to matters in which he is interested. I must confess that his tenacity was not substantially rewarded on this occasion. He asked further questions, and let me repeat one of them, as recorded on the same page of Hansard of that date:
Has the minister any idea of the total cost of the building?
That would seem like a fairly important question in dealing with a matter of this kind. The minister replied in these words:
I am told that right now they think that the building will cost $5 million, but we have not got the plans and it is quite difficult for me to make an estimate.
It must have been rather difficult for him to make an estimate when the estimates were being prepared, because it was obviously not based on any plan.

The Address-Mr. Drew Then the hon. member tor Peterborough asked the following question, which seemed like a very sensible question to ask and which does indicate that the members of this house were interested in finding out what was happening. This question is recorded on the same page of Hansard:
What will the site cost on top of that?
This would seem like the question of a cautious person interested in public affairs; and this is big business, the business of the country. To that the Minister of Public Works replied, and one could almost see the bland expression with which he answered:
I cannot give an estimate for the building before the plans and specifications are prepared and I cannot say whether the site will be comprised in that amount. We have not completed the purchase of the land and I would not like to give the figures I have here at this time.
That was the last time, Mr. Speaker, there was even any pretence of giving information, if you could call this information. This matter of great importance to the people of Canada, whom we collectively represent, had not been sufficiently explored to give even the most elementary information to the house and through this house to the people of Canada whose money will be spent. No indication was given as to why this move was being made. There was no indication as to why the recommendations of the committee of the house were being disregarded. There was no indication why the headquarters was going to be at Ottawa and the operations in Montreal, perpetuating some of the very difficulties pointed out by J. D. Woods and Gordon. There was no indication why a site was chosen which, according to common report, may call for certain soundproof equipment to make it possible to operate in that particular area. In fact there was no information of any kind upon which this or any other legislative body could possibly be said to have formed a decision.
There were a lot of other equally uncertain answers. I have not given all the answers, but they were just as vague, just as uncertain and just as meaningless. However, that was the decision of parliament to which reference has been made. Unfortunately this is only too vivid an illustration of what happens when the government takes over some of these operations which, although excellent in themselves, are then placed behind a veil. We must not ask too much about them in case it be suggested that we are showing undue interest in the private activities of those who might be engaged in the same business.
What did J. D. Woods and Gordon mean when they said the work of the board in 

Ottawa should be centralized and suitable accommodation provided? As I read those words they contemplated that this operation would remain in Ottawa and a site would be found to accommodate the whole operation under one roof.
Every remark I make now is directed to the whole question of the operation of public activities of this kind, and to the type of information the members of this house should have before a final decision is made. I am not referring to the film board alone. I am taking this as an example because only yesterday in this house we had the suggestion that there is something very improper if anyone begins to ask questions about these operations which the government undertakes. I grant you that on that occasion it was not a supporter of the government who made the remarks to which I refer.
Certainly administration is part of the operations of the board; and certainly if these recommendations mean anything they should be brought together. Why are they not all brought together? We still have a right to know that. In fact it seems, from the discussions which took place earlier, that the very key to the success of the operation was to bring everything together in one comprehensive operation.
There was one other occasion when one may say there was reference to this subject. That was the day before the last session of the last parliament closed. Just as a reminder to hon. members of how this process of frustration finally works, I would refer to Hansard of May 13 of this year, when the supplementary estimates dealing with the film board, which were shown as Nos. 247 and 248, were announced. The house was about to close, or the session was about to close, and the process of exhaustion had won its weary battle. Therefore we find the last reference to this subject:

And it was carried. That was the last reference to it. That was what took place in dealing with this very important subject. Yes, we are all to blame; we are all to blame to the extent that we are not prepared to sit here debating months on end just in the hope of delaying the passage of an item of this kind, because no other process is available to us.
Every time the question was asked, "What are the plans?", the answer was "There are

no plans." "Have you acquired a site?" "It is not settled yet". "What is the policy?" "I don't know whether I can answer that. You are merely members of parliament. You are merely elected representatives of the people. It is not your business. Go home; we are tired of you." That is the way this has operated. And I repeat that we are all to blame. But therein we have one perfect example of why we need some committee on estimates, why this particular subject should be brought back to the house to be examined. This series of questions and answers illustrates what took place on this particular occasion.
We do not know anything yet about the total cost. The minister did not like to give us the figures because he did not have the plans. That may not seem too strange, in a way. But what is the total cost? Is it $10 million? Is it $15 million? We do not know, and the government did not know at that time, the last time it was discussed. We know nothing about the reasons for the board's decision. We certainly have no information as to why the government is going to go directly against the report of the business experts it engaged, and that of a committee of the house. We do not know why it is to be built in a place so noisy that special devices will have to be introduced to suppress that noise. Were there not compensating factors in some other site where that problem would not have arisen?
It is not a question as to the desirability of Montreal. It is a question of the desirability of knowing what the facts are. The only suggestion by way of a reason is that Montreal is the centre of bilingual culture. But, Mr. Speaker, I was under the impression that Ottawa was also a centre of bilingual culture. And I think we have seen increasing evidence to the effect that not only is it a centre of bilingual culture but that it is the centre of an increasing effort to do business in this country in both languages.
No, Mr. Speaker, we have no evidence of any kind before us yet. But this is something that goes far beyond the question of whether or not a site in Ottawa or in Ville St. Laurent is the proper one. This is something that goes to the root of the whole question of the operation of public activities of this kind. Of course it may be suggested that any argument that we should weigh the facts is an argument in favour of private film industry in Canada. Surely we will not hear chestnuts of that kind. We believe and we have no hesitation in saying that we believe in the value of private initiative and of personal skill and of personal drive in building up this or any other industry.
The Address-Mr. Drew Never has it been suggested that the national film board was intended to mean the nationalization of the film industry in Canada. If that is the intention, then let it be said. But it has never been said yet.
If that is not the intention, then let us be sure the field is still open for private industry to build up film production in Canada within its own field. That, after all, is the basis of competition, in which we have expressed our belief. But do not let anyone in this house, Mr. Speaker, permit the impression to be conveyed that it is only the national film board which has produced excellent films. Splendid films which have been recognized by awards outside of Canada, in different parts of the world, have been produced by the private film industry in this country, and they should be encouraged.
They should be encouraged by having the fields of public and private activity clearly defined. One thing we do not know, one thing about which we have received no hint at any time, is what really are the terms of reference to the film board, and what they have been told they should do. Before any decision is carried to its conclusion this house should know just exactly how far the national film board is to go, and whether in fact it is going to go into the competitive production of films as well as produce the type of films it already produces.
I am not suggesting that it does, but we say we do not know. Let us be sure whether it be in this, or in the operations of the C.B.C.; whether it be television or radio or transportation, or in any other public activities, that the boundaries of public activity be clearly defined, and that members of this House of Commons, who represent the people of this country, know within what boundaries public funds are going to be expended.
I do suggest that this could be done in the most satisfactory way by agreeing now to refer this matter to a committee of the house, so this could be discussed not merely from the point of view of this one problem but from the point of view of principles which are to apply to public ownership, when the government enters fields of activity of this kind. Mr. Speaker, if this is the kind of information that is to be regarded as information upon which decisions can be made in parliament, what is the use of our pretending to discuss these matters at all? If the information given in this case is to be regarded as adequate information, what is the use of setting up committees and pretending they can make proper recommendations to parliament itself?
Every one of these questions and answers points not only to the need for a committee

The Address-Mr. Drew to deal with this subject, but to the need for a comprehensive review of our whole method of dealing with the estimates and with legislation generally, to assure that in future committees of this house of parliament will have the kind of information they should have. At a time when we profess our belief in democracy in such vigorous terms, and support without hesitation all proper expenditures required to defend that democracy, let us be sure that the processes of democracy are vigorous, strong and effective, right here where the representatives of the people of Canada meet to do the business of the nation.
I suggest once again that this is not a case where there should be a setting up of some atmosphere of sanctity and a suggestion that just because the government has created this sacred cow we should all bend the knee and worship in abject reverence before this idol which the government has set up. I close these remarks with a repetition of the request and the suggestion that the evidence supports the reasons why I contend that this request should be granted.
I wish now to deal briefly with the subamendment on which we shall be called upon to vote. The subamendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and seconded by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) removed from the amendment we had presented the words "free competition" and substituted therefor the words "private enterprise" and further added to our amendment in regard to the restoration of markets and the expansion of international trade the words, "by the acceptance of sterling in payment therefor". The amendment as amended reads:
We respectfully represent to Your Excellency that the welfare of Canada Is dependent upon private enterprise; and that the prosperity and security of all Canadians will be advanced by government policies which will restore markets for primary products and generally promote a high volume of international trade by the acceptance of sterling in payment therefor.
I must confess that I am unable to understand from anything that has been said why it was deemed advisable to substitute the words "private enterprise" for the words "free competition" because I am under the impression that, in the ordinary use of words, free competition, free enterprise and private enterprise are synonymous terms.

notice that the hon. member for Peace River nods his head in assent so I assume that the hon. member who moved the subamendment agrees that he has not changed the effect of that part of the amendment but has simply substituted one similar term for another. That being the case-*

speechtext:
I think it does clarify the meaning of the words "free enterprise".
Mr. Drev/: I take it from the assent expressed a moment ago by the hon. member for Peace River that he agrees that in ordinary discussions they would be synonymous terms. The hon. member indicates that that is so. That being the situation, whatever refinements our friends to the immediate left may seek to apply to these terms, in the thoughts of those who moved the subamendment they are synonymous terms. I must be completely fair to the hon. member for Peace River and say that apparently he feels that the words "private enterprise" more clearly express the meaning he wishes to convey. I am not going to quarrel in any way with that contention. I agree that in ordinary use the words "free enterprise" and "private enterprise" are perhaps more frequently used and perhaps are better understood. I think that free competition is an even wider term, but in any event I think they are all synonymous and mean freedom, and just that.	.
I think that freedom is an indivisible term and that what we are talking about is freedom of the individual to carry on his own business, either as an individual or with others collectively, according to his own ideas within the framework of just and equitable laws which will prevent abuses and permit the individual or groups of individuals to take his or their risks and seek the reward that comes with risk and the profits that are an encouragement to take such risks. That is what has built up this country and other countries which have grown greatly in these past few years. Therefore we do not seriously question that, although we do wonder why it was thought necessary to change the wording.
We come now to the words used at the end of the subamendment, "by the acceptance of sterling in payment therefor." The party which I have the honour to lead in this house has been constant in its demands that this government take the initiative in seeking convertibility of sterling and dollars so that what we have described as the log jam of non-convertibility may be broken. I do not suggest any exclusive virtue in this respect on our part, but I do say most emphatically that no party in this house has been more consistent in its demands that

everything possible be done to maintain, to expand and to increase our trade with the United Kingdom, the nations of the commonwealth and the sterling area generally.
We have introduced resolution after resolution to that effect and those resolutions have been voted down by the supporters of the government. I want to read just one or two of those resolutions to indicate the consistency of our position in this respect. On October 21, 1949, as reported on page 1023 of Hansard, the following resolution was moved by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and seconded by the then hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris):
That all the words oE the resolution after the first word "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
this house regrets that the government has failed to take effective measures to prevent the present decline in our trade with the sterling area and is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of inviting the nations of the commonwealth to a conference in the immediate future for the purpose of working out arrangements to preserve and enlarge those traditional markets on which jobs and opportunities for Canadians very largely depend.
That motion was voted down by the supporters of the government. Every member of the Liberal party voted against it.

It is open to the government at any time to accept suggestions from the opposition, particularly when the opposition indicates, as it did on this and other occasions, that it is quite prepared to have the government act and not have the suggestion treated as a want of confidence motion. That has been suggested over and over again. We have made it clear that we were asking, first, that the government act in this matter. Whether the government in one particular case can or cannot point to an example where that was not done, the government at all times had it within its power to say, "If this is not to be regarded as a want of confidence motion, and the members of the house will support it, without regarding it as a want of confidence motion, it can be treated in that way." That is a parliamentary practice, and we would have been ready to accord that tonight. In so far as that is concerned, again in 1950 there was a resolution dated February 28, as recorded at page 308 of Hansard, and I quote:
this house is of the opinion that the government should take immediate steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth and the countries of the empire to devise policies to restore our lost markets, and thereby to provide jobs for our Canadian people.
The Address-Mr. Drew
In that case again it was an amendment by the Conservative party and it was voted down solidly by the members of the Liberal party in the house at that time. Then, on June 3, 1952, there was a resolution moved by myself and seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), and I quote from page 2853 of Hansard of that date:
this house is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of taking steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth to seek means by which there may be convertibility of commonwealth currencies, and to explore all the possibilities for restoring and enlarging those traditional markets upon which our prosperity so largely depends.
I read these resolutions, Mr. Speaker, because we have been insisting over and over again that steps be taken to produce effective convertibility between sterling and dollars. It may be recalled by some that the genial Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) treated with some ridicule these suggestions that this could be done. Now, I am happy to find that, with some measure of satisfaction, he announces that he will proceed to Australia in January to discuss this very subject. I regret that our proposal was not accepted four years ago, and I also regret that the initiative was not Canada's initiative, and that the meeting is not going to take place here in Ottawa where we can act as the great interpreter between the United Kingdom and the United States. I would also point out that every Liberal member in the house voted against that latter motion.
We believe, Mr. Speaker, in the future of the United Kingdom; we believe in the future of the commonwealth of nations; we believe that every possible step should be taken to recognize that, sentiment apart, this great partnership presents immense opportunities for profitable trade to Canada as well as to the other nations of the commonwealth. We have asserted our belief over and over again that this is not a mere question of sentiment, affection or loyalty. We have made it clear that while we certainly believe that all these have a place, and a very important place, this is also a matter of good business for Canada.
We have pointed out the traditional place of the United Kingdom as a market for Canadian foodstuffs, Canadian raw materials and Canadian products of various kinds. Never once, however, have we suggested that we should not trade in every way we can with our great neighbour to the south-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that was before the hon. member was in the house and long before I was in the house. I do not know if that was ever said in this house. I am talking about what we have been dealing with here at the present time. I have no doubt that the statement referred to by the hon. member is one of these comforting statements that are treasured to be used on occasions when other statements of that kind, brought out of the past, seem to give such a measure of satisfaction to certain members of the party across the floor.
These resolutions speak for themselves and there is no member of this house who has been following this debate who is in any doubt about the fact that we want trade with the United States, as well as with the United Kingdom and the nations of the commonwealth and the sterling area generally. We have said, and we do not hesitate to repeat it, that we do not want all our eggs in one basket, and we also do not hesitate to repeat that when it comes to using resources which could be employed for the purpose of giving employment to young Canadians in Canada instead of giving employment in the United States, we think the first consideration should be for Canadians.
But that is not to be interpreted by any reasonable person as denying the principle of trade on a sound basis which shall respect the rights of our own people to the proper use of those resources which God has given us for our own particular trust. In fact, I find that we had support for that principle from the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) a few days ago, and when we receive support for this principle from any quarter in this house I think there is no reason why we should not indicate our acceptance of the support of our arguments along that line.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to come to the effect of these words. It is appealing to suggest that we accept sterling, but I want to emphasize exactly what the words are, and I quote from page 386 of Hansard dated November 26, 1953:
. . . that the prosperity and security of all Canadians will be advanced by government policies which will restore markets for primary products and generally promote a high volume of international trade by the acceptance of sterling in payment therefor.
That is not very clear. We hope that out of the meetings in January some method may


be found by which sterling may be really convertible. However, I think it must be said that the objective of all members, now that the government has come to this view itself, is convertibility. We want convertibility. We want sterling as freely exchanged for dollars in Canada as it was in days gone by. We have indicated our belief that Canada should be prepared to take some risks in that respect which will be related to its confidence in the United Kingdom and the commonwealth partnership generally.
But, Mr. Speaker, surely it is appropriate that we ask ourselves, at the same time that we are called upon to vote on an amendment to our own amendment which we have presented in regard to trade, just what the effect of these words really is. The words, as they read, imply that we are going to solve the problems of international trade by accepting sterling; and that, as one interprets the words, would seem to be sterling currency. Mr. Speaker, there is a vast difference between making arrangements which will permit the interchange of sterling and dollars and entering into an open-end arrangement for the acceptance of sterling which we have reason to doubt the British government would itself be prepared to enter into at this time.
One of the things which the British government has been making very clear is that it wants trade, not aid. One of the things which the British government has been making very clear is that it wants convertibility. Another thing they have been making very clear is that they have to get some control over the sterling now loose if they are going to be able to achieve convertibility. There is no evidence that this proposal has been submitted to the government of the United Kingdom, and I would be extremely doubtful whether the government of the United Kingdom would feel that any such arrangement was workable. On the contrary, I am inclined to think that any open-end arrangement under which sterling was to be taken for purchases, without some specific plan, would in itself delay the day when these currencies might become convertible.
I grant that these are debatable subjects; but we have not had the proposals defined to us in terms that we can understand. One thing which perhaps caused some concern in the minds of many Canadians was that press reports from the United States conveyed the impression that the government of the United States was going to accept up to $250 million in soft currencies, for foodstuffs of different kinds, from friendly nations. That is not the arrangement. The proposal which was referred to in these reports which created the impression that the

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
United States was going to take sterling and other soft currencies for foodstuffs was, in fact, an amendment to the Mutual Security Act and is known as the Mutual Security Act of 1953. Under section 550 of that act of the congress of the United States it is provided as follows:
Not less than $100 million and not more than $250 millicn of the funds authorized to be appropriated under this act shall be used, directly or indirectly, to finance the purchase of surplus agricultural commodities, or products thereof, produced in the United States.
What that means is that the United States congress is setting aside $100 million to $250 million to purchase their own foodstuffs and to make them available to the soft currency countries. Then there is a further provision in regard to that matter. It is provided that the local currency made available in that way is to be spent for military projects; and those military projects are such projects as the extension of air bases and other details of that kind. In brief, what this act really amounts to is a procedure by which the government of the United States disposes of some of its surplus food products and, in the process, furthers its declared objectives of creating increased defence strength in those friendly nations with which agreements are made. There is no question whatever about the United States government's accepting sterling and getting it in the form of currency; none whatever. It has nothing to do with special prices or anything of that kind. It is simply a case of injecting into the mutual security aid program, to the possible extent of a quarter of a billion dollars, this two-pronged process of delivering farm products and getting certain defence projects carried to completion.
Mr. Speaker, may I make it perfectly clear that I personally would be happy to hear discussed any specific proposal of this nature. Whether we could support it or not would, of course, depend upon the terms in which it was presented and how the proposal was to be carried out. Most certainly, if there is some specific proposal that will aid in the sale of surplus stores of wheat or of other grain or of other food, let us have that proposal made in definite form. Also, Mr. Speaker, may I emphasize that we would welcome-and we said that at the outset- any suggestion by this government for some plan by which they can speed up the movement of that surplus grain which now lies in such large quantities on the farms of western Canada. This is something above politics. It is something above any sectional consideration. This is something that affects
the whole national economy. We would welcome those suggestions. But, Mr. Speaker, before supporting a resolution of this kind simply because the general purpose seems to be attractive, we surely must ask ourselves these questions: Is it practical? Is it sensible? Is it workable? Is there any evidence whatever that the other party to the proposal would be inclined to accept the proposal if it were made?
I should think that everything that has been said by the Chancellor of the Exchequer of the United Kingdom would make it perfectly clear to us that they would be disinclined to accept any such open-end proposal. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, believing that we should do everything humanly possible to achieve convertibility of sterling and dollars, and believing that we should do everything humanly possible to expand trade between the nations of the commonwealth and Canada as well as with every other trading nation of the free world, may I say that I do not believe that I personally can see any practical effect to this particular motion which makes it possible for me to support it. Therefore, personally, I shall vote against the subamendment that is now presented.
