Mr. Speaker, it is my purpose this evening to present to the house a few facts pertaining to Owen Lattimore, one of the men whom Senator McCarthy has searched out in the United States administration and exposed as a key figure in the communist organization of that country. Before I proceed, may I point out to the country at large a thing which I think is not generally understood in this house or in the country, namely, that the whole matter at issue in Senator McCarthy's struggle is whether or not it is going to be possible to remove from the United States administration the communists who are endeavouring to shape American policy to agree with the policy of Russia. It is not all of this other nonsense that we hear talked about. That is the whole matter. McCarthy, as I said not very long ago, is a great anti-communist


crusader, and that is all there is to it. Because he is bringing communists down, opposition has been raised against him as it always is when anybody successfully attempts to strike a blow at the communist organization.
It may be asked, what has Lattimore to do with Canada? Is he not strictly a United States problem?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I ask hon. members this question. Did it or did it not affect Canada when China went behind the iron curtain and under the iron heel of communism and was turned from a friend into a dangerous potential enemy? I ask hon. members if that had no effect on their children and their children's children.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We do not
know yet.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is a pretty safe bet that when 400 million people are taken away from your side and put on the other side it throws that many more people against you. It does not take much arithmetic to see that, does it? Does it make to Canada no difference that China, with her more than 400 million people, an almost limitless pool of manpower upon which communist Russia has already freely drawn; that China, a potential industrial nation of great power; that China, the control of which brings Russia perilously close to Japan and America, has gone behind the iron curtain? Again I ask whether it was not a matter of concern to Canada when the free world lost China.
What had Lattimore to do with the loss of China to America? I read a statement just before the house took recess to show what he had to do with it. He said in effect that the problem of the United States administration, if you please, the state department, the Far Eastern administration, was to lose China to communism without letting the American people realize that America had pushed China under communism.
The word "traitor" just breaks down when one attempts to use it to describe a man who would do a thing of that kind. It appears that Lattimore was one of the key agents, if not the main agent, in pushing China into communist hands. Lattimore was a highly intelligent man who called himself a foreign affairs expert. He was often called the architect of United States Far Eastern policy. Did Lattimore's part in this nefarious performance with respect to China affect Canada? Has it already affected Canadian boys who went to fight in defence of Korea and found themselves overwhelmed by vast, seething hordes of men who could bear them down if

they only used their claws and no other weapons? Did that make a difference to us? I imagine it would.
Has anything occurred since 1945 that should concern this house and the nation more? Before the house took recess I read a short passage from an article by Lattimore which said that the chief problem of the administration in respect of Korea is to let Korea fall without letting the American people know that we pushed her. Hon. members are wondering why Syngman Rhee is making such a determined stand. A little bit of careful study and reading between the lines will help all hon. members to see that what Syngman Rhee is desperately struggling against is that very thing that Lattimore maintains was the chief object of United States foreign policy and the American state department.
These things are not among Canadians generally understood, but it is not going to be very long before they will be understood, and I hope we understand them before it is too late. That is what the fight over McCarthy is all about. I ask hon. members: Did the Korean trouble affect Canada? If South Korea were in real danger of being manoeuvred into communist hands right now would that affect Canada? We have set aside something like $2 billion a year presumably to fight communism in Korea. If that is to be in vain, together with all the men whose lives are thrown away, is anyone going to pretend that is not a matter of serious concern to Canada and should not be a topranking topic for discussion in the throne debate right in the house? After thinking about it I do not imagine any hon. member would venture to say that it was not a matter of serious concern.
It may be said that all this is happening over in the United States. But we are intimately bound up with the United States in the defence of this continent. If the United States falls, Canada falls. Where the United States goes to fight, Canada is going to be more or less involved, as she has already been in Korea. What is the sense of voting $2 billion a year and imposing upon ourselves almost unbearable taxation only to see the fruits of victory for which we have made all this sacrifice filched away by clever manoeuvrers in the Far Eastern department of the United States administration? Let me give a timely tip to those who have not taken the trouble to study McCarthy and what he is struggling about. Let them read, let them get right down and get the facts, not what is scattered around in newspapers, because that is highly-paid propaganda. Let us remember that I am not so much out of

Tydings insisted on a public disclosure of names. The senator from Wisconsin, on February 20, 1950 repeatedly stated and restated on the floor of the Senate that he did not want to make names public; that, he would not tell the names to the Senate in public.

When Senator McCarthy was pressed for the names in the Senate he said that the names were available to the senators if they cared to have them, but if they should label one man a communist when he was not a communist it would be too bad. I will ask no more. All I wish is to bring this case, which is of very great importance, to members of the house and country at the present time; because it shows the methods used. When I have finished-and I shall not be more than two or three minutes more-I shall close that part of my speech and go on to another subject which I am anxious to talk about tonight.
McCarthy told the Tydings committee that he must give names in order to present his case. He said he would have to name names in the committee. The committee voted to hold open sessions, which meant that they were going to force Senator McCarthy to give names in public, without having proof established.
McCarthy then gave each of the pressmen a copy of his testimony on the Kenyon case. If he was going to give the committee the material anyway, he might as well put it in the hands of the press, so that they would have it straight. As soon as Tydings saw
The Address-Mr. Blackmore that the details of the Kenyon case were already in the hands of the press, and therefore the hands of the public, Tydings offered to allow McCarthy to testify in executive session.
Hon. members and people throughout the country will readily discern how easy it thus became for Tydings or any other opponent to misrepresent McCarthy's methods in respect of Kenyon, one of his cases, before the Tydings committee. It will readily be discerned also that, most people of the country not being able to learn or even to understand the technicalities of the circumstances, it would be wellnigh impossible for Senator McCarthy or his friends to answer the misrepresentations beyond possibility of question. That is, a sort of contemptible trick was used. People will see such a thing happen, and the interpretation may be at variance with what it ought to be because the people do not understand the rules under which it was done.
Thus we see the reason for Mr. Tydings' cleverly deceptive gesture as regards the Kenyon case. The Tydings committee heard the evidence on only nine of McCarthy's cases, and then it decided to hear the remainder in closed session. This was done after a number had been held in open session, so McCarthy's enemies could blame McCarthy for trying to smear those whom he investigated.
The Lattimore case came up first in closed session. Then the committee did not allow McCarthy to present any more cases in executive session. McCarthy insisted upon, and had, a strict understanding that Latti-more's name would not be divulged to the public by the committee until his case had been fully investigated.
Who, then, made Lattimore's case public? Drew Pearson made Lattimore's name public. According to Owen Lattimore's book "Ordeal by Slander," Mrs. Lattimore wrote to him on March 26, 1950. Drew Pearson's broadcast really "broke the story". You see the trick played there?
Lattimore's book "Ordeal by Slander" reveals the fact that Lattimore's lawyer, Abe Fortas, knowing beforehand that Lattimore's name would be made public in this broadcast, invited Mrs. Lattimore to listen to the broadcast. If you want a dirty sort of trick, there you have it. It appears that Drew Pearson, upon the advice of Lattimore's lawyer, Abe Fortas, deliberately made Lattimore's name public and then started running a smear campaign against McCarthy, claiming that McCarthy "had publicly smeared Owen Lattimore under the cloak of congressional immunity". Now, can you think

The Address-Mr. Blackmore of a dirtier trick than that to play on any person? And that is the sort of thing we have been listening to in Canada.
Drew Pearson charged McCarthy with having publicly smeared Owen Lattimore under the cloak of congressional immunity. Owen Lattimore challenged McCarthy to make his statements about Lattimore outside the Senate, and out from under the protection of congressional immunity, so that Lattimore could sue McCarthy. McCarthy offered to waive immunity if Lattimore would consent to have the legal evidence in Lattimore's F.B.I. file made available in any lawsuit which Lattimore might start.
Now what does Lattimore do? Senator Hickenlooper during the Tydings hearings asked Lattimore if he would be willing to have the legal evidence in his file made available. Mr. Lattimore refused to ask that his file be made available on the ground that, in his words, "I should be asking for a favour, and that I refuse to do". I suggest that hon. members should see the Tydings committee hearings of April 6, 1950, pages 483 and 484.
Lattimore's reply is not hard to appreciate, when we remember that Senator McCarthy, in presenting the Lattimore case to the Tydings committee, said that he was willing to stand or fall on the Lattimore case.
Now, there is the case; you can draw your own conclusions. So if hon. members will excuse me I shall not spend more time on this, but I shall proceed to some other things.

One paper is the Charleston News-Courier and the other is the News-Times of Hendersonville, North Carolina. You have newspapers in two states of the United States taking the same position. I could read them, but I shall leave them now and if anyone wishes to see them he may.
Before I take my seat I wish to say a word about an entirely different matter, namely the Waterton Lakes national park in southwestern Alberta. I feel that our parks in Canada are extremely important because of their influence upon tourist trade. This particular park is in my constituency and consequently I appreciate how important it is. As I said, it is located in southwestern Alberta and borders on British Columbia and Montana. It is just across the border from the Glacier national park in the United

States. These two parks have been combined idealistically to form what is known as the Waterton-Glacier international peace park.
The development of this park is considerably behind what it should be for reasons which I will not now go into. Its complete development has been delayed now for about twenty years and it is highly important that considerable money should be spent on the park immediately in order to bring it up to the standard it warrants.
This is an extremely interesting park to tourists and great numbers come to visit it in increasing numbers every year. If we can attract tourists with high-class parks then we shall be in position to tap the source of American dollars provided by tourists to this country.
This park contains many wonderful lakes. There are the Waterton lakes and I do not think any more beautiful lakes can be found anywhere in Canada. There is the delightful Cameron lake, the Carthew lakes, Bertha lake and Wall lake. They are all exceedingly beautiful, nestling among mountains of extreme beauty. These lakes fall just short of equalling the beauty of the famous lake Louise in Banff.
There are two beautiful falls in the park, Cameron falls and Blakiston falls. Either one of these falls is worth going 500 miles to see. There are a number of beautiful creeks such as Cameron creek, Pass creek, Red Rock canyon and Blakiston creek.
The park contains many types of animals such as mountain goats and mountain sheep, white-tailed deer, mule deer, red deer, black bears, brown bears, grizzly bears, cinnamon bears and elk. There is a buffalo paddock containing a number of fine buffalo roaming around just as their forebears did long ago. There are great numbers of fish in the park; in fact it is one of the most valuable fishing resorts to be found anywhere. With a little more money being spent it could be made even better.
There are mountains of remarkable beauty, lofty, rugged, colourful and unique in their general appearance. They would be an inspiration to anyone.
The park contains many good roads. There are hard-surfaced roads in the townsite. The Waterton-Pincher road is almost all hardsurfaced now. The Waterton-Carway road is almost all hard-surfaced. The road to Cardston is all ready to be hard-surfaced and the Cardston-Lethbridge road is already hard-surfaced.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity which the procedure followed by this House of Commons gives to an hon. member to rise on various amendments if he feels that something should be brought immediately to the attention of the government. I assure hon. members that it is not my intention to abuse that privilege. However, I do want to say that I do not agree with the view expressed by an hon. member on the other side or in certain editorials or by certain columnists, that there is too much talk during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In my estimation, I am not sent here by the electors of Vancouver East for the purpose of sitting on my
606	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Winch seat, and I use that word in the physical and not the constituency sense, and just drawing my cheque.
I consider this parliament as a board of directors of 265 conducting the biggest business in the Dominion of Canada, a business which has to raise and spend approximately $4,000 million a year. According to the way we vote on policies and legislation we affect the life of every man, woman and child in the Dominion of Canada. Therefore, it is our responsibility as members of that board of directors to speak if we feel we have something that should be said.
Over a period of centuries a parliamentary procedure has been laid down under which only the government can introduce legislation dealing with policy or with taxation or the expenditure of money. The debate on the throne speech and that on the budget afford the only opportunities a private member has of bringing to the attention of the government matters of policy or of legislation that he thinks should be introduced. I hope the government will give consideration and perhaps do something at this present session of parliament on the matters drawn to their attention. When I spoke a week ago last Tuesday I drew the attention of the government to three matters which I considered of importance. I now have an additional two points that I desire to draw to the notice of the house at this time. Before dealing with them, however, I would like to make a few comments upon the remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) who has just spoken.
I will not take up the time of the house in commenting on his charges, or in commenting on his attacks on individuals in other countries. I only want to deal with what I consider to be his approach, because I feel it is important that his approach should be commented upon.
After listening to him this afternoon I felt I had to refresh my memory on a report I read only this morning in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix dated Saturday, November 28. When I read that report this morning I thought it was something of a joke, but after listening to the hon. member I think the matter is serious. It is not a joke because the item referred to in the Star-Phoenix seems to express an approach that is almost identical with that of the hon. member for Lethbridge. Let me quote from the Star-Phoenix of November 28 which deals with an election in the University of Saskatchewan. Most universities have students' political groups and they nearly all have a parliamentary forum

or mock parliament, and most of these university political groups discuss matters of the day and take politics very, very seriously, as they should. But apparently a change has come about in Saskatchewan, if the report in the newspaper I have mentioned is true, because they have just had an election in the University of Saskatchewan and according to the press more Social Credit candidates were elected than were elected from any of the other parties. But let me quote from page 3 of the newspaper I have mentioned:
A jclier party wins university election. A joker party under the name of Social Credit has won the parliamentary forum at the University of Saskatchewan. For several weeks before the election there has been much debate on the campus about whether the mock parliament should be kept on a serious political level.
Now, Mr. Speaker, at the same time that I saw this newspaper this morning there came into my hands another publication that I have never heard of before. It also is published in Saskatoon and it calls itself Straw 'n Chaff. In its write-up it completely substantiates what was in the newspaper I have just quoted from and it goes even further. It outlines the slogans, the platform and the policies of the various parties that ran. It states that the C.C.F., the Liberals, the Conservatives and other groups ran a campaign on the issues of the day and it set forth what they would do if elected. The Social Credit group went off on a completely new tack and I want to quote from this publication Straw 'n Chaff because I think it indicates, from what I have heard from the hon. member for Lethbridge this afternoon, their thinking and their approach and what their battlecry was in this election. The Social Credit battle-cry was, and I quote:
Arise, you idiots, you have nothing to lose but your brains.
And it goes on:
Culminating in a spirited campaign which placed the issues squarely before the electorate the Socreds relied entirely on the desires of the student body to return the mock parliament to its original status of more mockery and less parliament.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that I took this as a joke. But I think it is serious when I find in the same publication a statement by Mr. J. Haver, a Social Crediter and federal candidate for the constituency of Saskatoon in 1953 and a member of the-

speechtext:
I am quoting from a publication I found here in this house. This publication refers to the election iat the University of Saskatchewan and I am quoting from it and when I say quote, I mean exactly that. The statement of Mr. Havers reads, and I quote from this publication:
I would like to extend to Mr. Spencer and his colleagues my sincere congratulations on their outstanding victory for Social Credit at the university polls. They have done an excellent job and it proves what thinking men and women can do when they are not only aware of, but also imbued with the desire to correct, the flaws in the present economic system.
This being in quotes I take it this is a direct statement by a candidate for the Social Credit party in the last election. I say, sir, that this is not a good approach. If all this is a joke, then it is in bad taste. If Mr. Havers did not make such a statement then it should be repudiated because it is of the utmost importance that in what we say on the floor of this parliament, and in the manner in which we conduct ourselves outside this parliament, we should maintain a respect for democracy, a respect for parliamentary institutions, and a respect for those who are elected to parliament irrespective of their political affiliations.
If we ever allow through our actions in this house or out of it a feeling of disrespect or cynicism to get abroad then we are laying the groundwork for a situation which could only coincide with what took place in Germany and Italy, and which, because of a feeling of cynicism and disrespect for parliament and members of parliament, led to the establishment of nazism and fascism.
I have felt it a great privilege, Mr. Speaker, to listen to all of the debates this past three weeks. I have learned a great deal. I have at the moment only two slight disappointments-no, not slight. One is a great disappointment and that is that unfortunately I do not have a knowledge of French. I regret very much that in my schooling I was taught Latin instead of French and I want to say that my lack of knowledge of the French tongue has been a great handicap. But, I assure the French-speaking members of the house I do not like sitting here out of courtesy listening to them and not knowing what they are saying and having to wait for French translations in Hansard, and may I assure them, Mr. Speaker, that it is my hope that in the not too distant future I will be able to sit here and understand what they are saying when they are saying it.
May I also comment on the system of oral questioning which I am not quite used to. I could not help noticing the great courtesy with which the majority of cabinet ministers
The Address-Mr. Winch answered questions and the explicit manner in which they answered them. That is true in the majority of cases but unfortunately there are one or two about whom I cannot make the same statement, and in my opinion they are a little bit evasive in some of their answers and sometimes more than evasive. In western Canada there is a word that is now coming into use and it is known as "weaseling". Now, "weaseling" has a political interpretation in two ways. First of all, it means saying something when you do not say "yes" and you do not say "no"; secondly, it means answering a question without giving any information. There are certainly one or two here who answer questions without giving any information. In particular I refer to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). I certainly hope that he follows the example of the majority of his colleagues and gets away from his own expression.
I said, sir, that there were two additional matters that I wanted to raise at this time. I want to add my voice to the words that have been spoken by members, I think, from all parties in this house asking the government to recognize the need for thinking about and for formulating some policy of decentralization of industry in the Dominion of Canada. There can be no question that the future prosperity of Canada depends upon an over-all, well-rounded system. We cannot have that if we have a concentration of industry in two provinces in Canada or if we have a concentration of industry in two of the large cities or centres of a province.
Decentralization is a major requirement at the present time. One way in which I believe something could be done about it is for the government to make a full and complete study of the system of industrial estates as it operates in Great Britain. I believe a few years ago in Great Britain a major advance was made when they recognized that they had depressed areas, that they had to decentralize industry. The government took the initiative in analysing the over-all picture in that country and then moved into the areas requiring attention. The government built the factories, the offices and the homes, put in the streets, the waterworks and the electric lights. Then the government went out with a definite plan of getting new industries established and of getting established industries to move from the centres of industry, of getting them to open branches and of assisting anyone who had a good idea, one which the government thought was practical, to have a factory in which to operate. They rented those establishments-and there are several now in Great Britain-on the basis
608	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Winch of one shilling a square foot a year. When I was in Great Britain in 1949 it was my privilege to go into a number of those establishments. As I have said before, I think they are a major step forward. I believe it would be in the interests of Canada if the present government would give consideration to the initiation of a similar plan in this dominion.
There is just one other point to which I wish to refer. I said that I was not going to abuse the privilege which is mine and I shall not do so. I raise this point at this time because I believe it is something upon which the government should take immediate action. I believe that more encouragement should be given to Canadian industry and that greater interest should be taken in seeing to it that Canadian industry gets a greater break in the supply of materials and in contracting for work when there is a mutual Canadian-United States agreement, and particularly when it is a mutual agreement for defence.
I am under no circumstances criticizing or attacking the principle of mutual agreements between the United States and the Dominion of Canada; but, Mr. Speaker, I think that we in Canada are not getting a break in the supply of materials and on tendering for contracts for work which is to be done in the Dominion of Canada. I realize that it would not be fair to generalize in that way so I am going to bring it down to a particular instance. I want to refer to the agreement made between the Dominion of Canada and the United States on what is known as the Haines-Fairbanks pipe line. The Haines-Fairbanks pipe line is under the permanent joint board on defence. It is being financed in the main by the United States government. Therefore it is a United States project. But in this project, a few hundred miles of it have to go through the province of British Columbia on the northern boundary. Not only in Canada a signatory, as she must be, to this project but Canada also has some responsibilities. In the agreement which was filed in this house we find paragraph 1 which is entitled "Right of Way" and which reads as follows:
All land or interest in land required for the right of way of the pipe line and appurtenances including any pumping stations . . . and for access roads, will be acquired by and remain in the title of Canada. Any expense incurred in the acquisition of such land shall be assumed by Canada.
Hence the dominion obviously has a financial as well as a defence interest in the Haines-Fairbanks pipe line. Because this is a mutual defence project, Canada moved very quickly to put through the necessary regulations in order to make it possible for all the equipment and all the supplies


coming into Canada from the government of the United States, from anyone who is contracting with the government of the United States or any Canadian who is contracting with the government of the United States, to come into Canada, as the memorandum says, free of customs duties, sales tax and excise tax. Canada moved very swiftly because, under date of September 18, the memorandum was sent out by the customs and excise division making it clear to all those concerned that Canada was not going to charge any customs duties, excise tax or sales tax on materials coming into British Columbia for this project.
The four or five weeks before I came down to the House of Commons I spent in making a survey of industry in British Columbia for the purpose of trying to be a better member of parliament by knowing the industries, what they are doing, what they can do, and what their potentialities are. In making that survey, Mr. Speaker, time after time I came up against a big industry who said they were interested in being able to tender on this Canadian-United States project but that they did not know what was going to happen on the sales tax and the customs duty position and that they did not know whom to contact. As soon as I came to Ottawa I tried to find out. I found out from the departments here in Ottawa that it is extremely easy to find out what Canada has done-which, as I have already pointed out, has been absolutely fair, absolutely decent-working in a speedy manner. But, Mr. Speaker, it took me five days to find out, or rather for the government departments to find out what the United States has done to give us equal treatment. I finally got the answer right here in Ottawa after five days' search; and the answer was that the United States has not given our people the same rights and the same treatment in tendering for supplies, work or materials in the contiguous sections in the United States. I think it is wrong that we have this kind of agreement, when part of a project goes through the Dominion of Canada, whereby we should say that the United States is exempt on anything that they send in but our people are not exempt from United States taxes if we want to bid on contiguous sections in the United States.

Canada has to pay for the acquisition of land in British Columbia. I do not know what that means if the United States pays the whole cost. If they are paying the whole cost, that is fine. I will accept that statement, even though it is outside the terms of the agreement. But they are in Canada. Because it is a mutual agreement we agreed to let them come in free of customs duties, sales tax and excise tax. I say that is as it should be. But I also say, sir, that the Canadian industries and Canadian products should have the same right in that contiguous section of the United States. It should be a twoway street, not a one-way street. I sincerely hope the government will take this matter under advisement. I am also certain that the minister, who has just spoken, will say that they are interested in encouraging the use of Canadian materials and that there is actually a section to that effect in the agreement. I want to be honest and fair so I will read it. It is subsection (c) of section 8 and reads as follows:
Canadian materials will be used on the Canadian portion of the line as far as feasible.
But we are in a pretty difficult position, as I have just outlined, because we are completely up against the competition of United States business concerns who want to come into Canada because they are operating on the same basis as Canadian firms, while on the other hand we are in a difficult position if we want to go into the United States unless the secretary of the army says that we do not have to pay these taxes. That is an impossible situation for industry to have to face if they want to tender on contracts for supplies. I said that the government will say they are very interested in this. I want to admit here and now that they have expressed their interest by the appointment of a civil servant to whom they have given the title of special commissioner on the Haines cut-off. He is the liaison officer with the United States officials on this pipe line in British Columbia.
That is as it should be, but here is the point. Before I left Vancouver I spent four or five weeks covering industry in that city, some of which are quite capable of tendering on this kind of job, and they did not know anything about this man who had been appointed. They had not heard of him. I found out as soon as I arrived here, and I want to say that I got the information speedily on my arrival. However, while this man may be the finest in the world, and I do not doubt but what he is, when I asked how industry was to get in touch with him I found that his postal address was Whitehorse, Yukon Territory.

All we are asking is an even break, and I ask for an even break for all Canadian industry. I am not speaking parochially for the province of British Columbia alone because the prosperity of Canada does not depend upon one province or community. It depends upon the prosperity of all Canada. All I am doing is asking that it be made clear that such agreements entail a two-way street irrespective of who is paying the shot, and that in appointing liaison officers such appointments should be well publicized and they should be stationed in a central location. That is all I want to say at this time on the matter of industrial estates, decentralization and these agreements. In addition, I hope that the government has not forgotten the matters I drew to their attention when I spoke last.

I am a little worried lest Liberal members of the house should be carried away completely by their worship of free enterprise and free competition and be induced to vote for this amendment and thereby bring about the defeat of their government. I just want to warn them-
Don't worry.

-what is entailed in

I suppose the Leader of the Opposition believes in what he says in the amendment. I presume he believes that the welfare of Canada depends upon free competition, and knowing as he does the extent to which free competition is at present non-existent in Canada he must be terribly worried about the welfare of Canada.
I gather from his speech and from that made by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) that the Progressive Conservative party is trying to resuscitate its fortunes by bringing the party back again to good old Tory policies. I suspect that they are getting tired of being out-Toried by the Liberals and are determined that they are going to find a place somewhere to the right of the Liberals if that is possible. From their speeches I would suggest that it is about time that they adopted a new name again for their party, and I would suggest instead of "Progressive Conservative" the name "Retrogressive Conservative party". I think that would express much better than the word "progressive" the line of policy that is being followed by their key speakers.
I do not know how serious the leader of the official opposition is when he implies in his amendment that we must get back to free competition. If he has any idea that we can come back to free competition again in this country I would say that his efforts to bring back free competition will be just as ineffective as were King Canute's efforts to hold back the tides of the ocean. The whole history of industry in modern times indicates that the so-called free enterprise system or private enterprise system or free competition system, all of which of course are sugar coatings for the ugly words "capitalist system", inevitably lead to monopolies, cartels and what is commonly known as big business.
I am sure that the leader of the official opposition and his supporters must have been


a little disappointed at the results of the reports made by the combines investigation commission since this session began. I have noticed that even chambers of commerce are beginning to point out that the commission is making a mistake when it tries to prosecute reliable and reputable business firms just because they form a combination to fix prices or to control sales. They realize that the day of free competition belongs to the time when businesses were small, when an individual owner owned his business and when his own capital was invested in it, not somebody else's capital.
The way in which business is conducted today renders it inevitable that there will be less and less of that free competition. The question which confronts us as a parliament is not whether or not to get back to free competition but who is to control these inevitable combines and cartels and big business associations. Are we going to leave the control entirely in the hands of the chairmen and presidents of these companies or are we going to entrust it, to some extent at least, to the hands of an agency of government that is responsible to the people of this country? I believe that is the question that we must face.
Now, just to indicate how utterly ridiculous is the official opposition's amendment regarding free competition, I am going to put on the record just one example of the kind 'of free competition we have in Canada today. I could, if time permitted, get examples of three or four men who control large sectors of our Canadian economy in which there is very little free competition. The one example I am going to put on the record is the case of one James Y. Murdoch, O.B.E., Q.C. I want to make it quite clear that I am not criticizing this reputable gentleman or his business. I am simply using this as an example of how little free competition there is today.
